opening: Lord, meet us gently today and always
body:
he words come from the Parable of the Prodigal Son in Gospel of Luke 15:29–30, when the older brother refuses to enter the celebration for the son who had returned home.

“All these years I served you. Not once did I disobey your orders. Yet you never gave me even a young goat to celebrate with my friends. But when this son of yours returns—after swallowing your property in reckless living—you slaughter the fattened calf for him.”

You can feel the frustration in his voice. Years of doing what was right. Years of staying, working, being faithful. And yet it seems the reward goes to the one who walked away. If we are honest, the older brother may feel uncomfortably familiar. Does he remind you of yourself at times? Have you ever felt as though you are doing everything you can—trying to be kind, neighborly, helping others where you can, attempting to live rightly—and yet the world seems to push back? Opportunities fall away. Doors close. Others seem to move ahead while you remain standing where you are. People will say they are “lucky.” I have never liked that word. What people often call luck may simply be gifts from God we do not yet recognize, grace unfolding in ways we do not fully see.

The older brother believed his obedience should guarantee something. Not necessarily wealth or applause, but at least some sense that his faithfulness mattered. Quietly, almost without noticing it, that feeling can turn into something else—entitlement. Entitlement is subtle. It does not always look arrogant. Sometimes it simply sounds like this: I did everything right… so why didn’t it work out for me? Perhaps we do not always recognize what entitlement feels like when it begins to grow inside us. Jesus tells this story so we can notice that temptation before it quietly hardens the heart.

The father answers him with remarkable gentleness: “My son, you are here with me always; everything I have is yours.” The father shifts the entire perspective. The real gift was never the goat, the feast, or the celebration. The gift was that the relationship had never been lost. The son had been home the entire time.

So perhaps this story invites us into a different way of seeing. When a door shuts, give thanks anyway. God is the one who holds the key, and there will always be other doors we cannot yet see. What feels like a loss today may simply be a path we were never meant to walk. Gratitude protects the heart from becoming hard. The tragedy of the story is not the younger son’s failure. The real tragedy would be the older brother standing outside the house, refusing to enter, while the feast of life continues inside.
